title: Data Archival Strategy
content:
Implementing a Data Archival Strategy with Amazon S3 and Glacier Overview In this lab, you will explore the basic concepts and hands-on steps involved in implementing a Data Archival Strategy using Amazon S3 in combination with S3 Glacier and Lifecycle Policies. The lab guides you through configuring automatic transitions of data from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier to optimize long-term storage costs. You will also learn how to enable Object Lock to protect data from accidental deletion.
Content Introduction Preparation EC2 Access Setup Configuring Lifecycle Policies Run and Results Clean up resources

title: Introduction
content:
Data Archival Strategy is a solution designed to optimize long-term storage for systems with infrequently accessed data that still needs to be preserved—such as personal blogs or digital publishing platforms.
In this project, i implemented a storage strategy for a blog microservice architecture using the following AWS services:
Amazon S3 Glacier for low-cost archival storage. Lifecycle Policy to automate transitions and scheduled deletions. Object Lock (compliance mode) to prevent deletion before retention time expires. By leveraging AWS archival storage services, you gain several key advantages:
Cost efficiency: Automatically moves outdated blog content to Glacier, which is significantly cheaper than S3 Standard. Automation: Lifecycle rules make it easy to manage object transitions and deletion based on time-based policies. Data protection: Object Lock ensures that archived content cannot be deleted or overwritten prematurely. Simplified management: S3’s user-friendly interface allows you to manage your archive without additional middleware. This approach is ideal for systems that:
Accumulate large volumes of content over time. Have stale or rarely accessed data after a period. Require cost savings without sacrificing data durability or compliance.

title: Create Lifecycle Rule
content:
Create Lifecycle Rule In this step, you will create a lifecycle rule with two actions applied to the objects.
Go to AWS BUCKET. Select the bucket you created earlier: blog-micro-data-archive. Switch to the Management tab. Click Create lifecycle rule to start. Next: Enter Lifecycle rule name: archive-to-glacier-and-delete. Set the Rule scope to Apply to all objects in the bucket. Check the confirmation box I acknowledge that this rule…. Check Transition current versions of objects between storage classes. Check Expire current versions of objects. Check the confirmation box I acknowledge that this lifecycle…. Then: Choose Storage class transitions: Glacier Flexible Retrieval (formerly Glacier). Set Days after object creation for transitioning storage class. Set the expiration time for the object versions, creating a delete marker after the object is created. Click Create rule to finish.

title: Create VPC
content: Create VPC Lab VPC Go to VPC service management console Click Your VPC. Click Create VPC. At the Create VPC page. In the Name tag field, enter Lab VPC. In the IPv4 CIDR field, enter: 10.10.0.0/16. Click Create VPC. While you may create a VPC as instructed above, I will be using the default VPC for this setup.

title: Open EC2 Ports
content: Open EC2 Ports Access the pageEC2. Click Instances. Select the instance named blogmicroservice. Select the Security tab. Click the link under Security groups. Next: Under Inbound rules, click Edit inbound rules. Click Add rule, set the Port range to 5672, and select Anywhere - IPv4 for the Source. Repeat for the Port range 15672. Click Save rules to apply the changes.

title: Preparation Steps
content:
To complete this lab, you need to have an S3 Bucket, IAM access with S3 permissions, and an EC2 instance prepared in advance.
Since I have applied this topic to my own project, you may need to download the project as well to perform this lab.
Before starting the implementation of the Data Archival Strategy, you should complete the following preparation steps:
Create an EC2 Instance. Create an S3 Bucket to store long-term data. Create an IAM User or Role with full access to Amazon S3. To learn how to create an S3 Bucket and configure permissions, refer to the following lab:
Working with Amazon S3 Contents Prepare VPC and EC2 Instance Create S3 Bucket Create IAM User

title: Create S3 Bucket
content:
Create S3 Bucket In this step, you will create an S3 Bucket to use for storing data in this lab.
Go to the AWS S3 Console. In the left navigation pane, select General purpose buckets. Click Create bucket. On the Create bucket page: Bucket type: select General purpose. Bucket name: enter blog-micro-data-archive. Object Ownership: select ACLs disabled. In the Block Public Access section, keep the default setting (leave Block all public access checked). In the Bucket key section, select Disable.
To enable Object Lock (prevent deletion or modification for a specific period of time):
In Advanced settings, under Object Lock, select Enable and check the confirmation box. Click Create bucket.

title: Create Subnet
content: Create Subnet Click Subnets. Click Create subnet. On the Create subnet page: In the VPC ID field, select the VPC you created earlier. In the Subnet name field, enter Subnet1. In the Availability Zone field, select the second availability zone. In the IPv4 CIDR block field, enter 172.31.0.0/28. Scroll down to the bottom of the page and click Create subnet.

title: Set Object Lock
content:
Set Object Lock To protect data from being deleted or modified, you need to set Object Lock for the bucket.
Go to Bucket. Inside the bucket, switch to the Properties tab. Find the Object Lock section and click Edit. Under Default retention, select Enable. For Default retention mode, choose Compliance. Set the object retention period. Click Save changes to apply.

title: Setup Docker & RabbitMQ
content:
Setup Docker & RabbitMQ Access the page EC2. Click Instances. Select the instance named blogmicroservice. Click Connect. On the Connect to instance page: Select the EC2 Instance Connect tab. Click Connect. Next, copy and paste each command below into the terminal: sudo apt-get update -y sudo apt-get install docker.io -y sudo systemctl enable docker sudo systemctl start docker sudo usermod -aG docker $USER newgrp docker docker run -d --hostname rabbitmq-host \ --name rabbitmq-container \ -e RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER=admin \ -e RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS=admin123 \ -p 5672:5672 \ -p 15672:15672 \ rabbitmq:3-management To list all containers, run:
docker ps -a
If the container already exists but is stopped, you can restart it by running:
docker start rabbitmq-container
Return EC2 Select the blogmicroservice instance. Copy the Public IPv4 address shown below. Open a new browser tab, paste the IP address, and append :15672. Enter Username: admin, Password: admin123. Click Login.

title: Configure .env Files
content:
Configure .env Files Open the previously downloaded project in Visual Studio Code. Go to the services directory. Here, you will see three services: user, author, and blog. Create a new .env file for each service. Based on the images below, create and add the required API configurations into the .env files. In the .env files for author and blog services, replace Rabbimq_Host with Public IPv4 address.

title: Create Access Key
content:
Create Access Key You have already created an IAM User in the previous steps.
In this section, you will create an access key to authenticate when sending data from your project.
Go to IAM Select the IAM User you created. Click Create access key. Continue: Select Command Line Interface. Check the confirmation box. Continue: Enter accesskey in the Description tag value field. Click Create access key. Continue: Click Download .csv file. Click Done to finish.

title: Create EC2 Ubuntu
content: Go to the EC2 Management Console Click Instances. Click Launch instances. On the Launch an instance page: In the Name field, enter blogmicroservice. In the Application and OS Images section under Quick Start, select Ubuntu. In the AMI field, choose Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, SSD Volume Type (Free Tier). Next: In the Instance type field, select t2.micro. In the Key pair name field, choose Create new key pair and set (type: RSA, format: .pem) if you do not already have one. In the VPC-required field, select the VPC created earlier. Continue: In the Auto-assign public IP field, select Enable. In the Firewall section, select Create security group. Click Launch instance to create.

title: Create IAM User
content:
Create IAM User In this step, you will create an IAM User with full access to the S3 Bucket.
Go to the AWS IAM Console. In the left navigation pane, select Users. Click Create user. On the Create user page:
User name: enter any name you want. Check the box Provide user access…. In the User type field, select I want to create an IAM user. In the Console password section:
To automatically generate a password, select Autogenerated password. To create your own password, select Custom password. If you want the user to set a new password upon first login, check Users must create a new password…. Click Next to proceed to Set permissions. On the Set permissions page: Under Permissions options, select Attach policies directly. Under Permissions policies, select AmazonS3FullAccess to grant full access to S3. Click Next to proceed to Review and create. Review the details and click Create user to complete. With this, the preparation steps are complete. Next, we will proceed to configure the ports and install packages for EC2.

title: Configuring Lifecycle Policies
content:
This is the main content of this Lab, with the goal of configuring Lifecycle Policies for an S3 Bucket.
This allows stored data files to automatically transition to different storage classes, leveraging the specific advantages of each class (cost, performance, or long-term archival).
In addition to automatic transitions, a Lifecycle Policy also supports various options such as deleting objects, expiring objects, or managing object versions based on a time period we define.
In this section, we will:
Create a Lifecycle rule: Configure the Transition current versions action: Move the storage class of current object versions to another storage class. Configure the Expire current versions action: Expire current versions and delete objects after a specified time. Set Object Lock: Prevent deletion or overwrite of an object for a specific period of time. Add IAM access keys: Create access keys for authentication when sending data from the project. In addition to the two main actions above, a Lifecycle Policy also supports:
- Transition noncurrent versions: Move noncurrent (older) versions of an object to another storage class.
- Permanently delete noncurrent versions: Permanently delete noncurrent versions.
- Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart uploads: Remove expired delete markers or unfinished multipart uploads.

title: Run and Results
content:
This section demonstrates running the project and reviewing the obtained results. It includes outcomes related to preventing deletion or modification through Object Lock, as well as automatic storage class transitions and object version expiration using Lifecycle Policies.
You need to run npm install and npm run build, then npm run dev for each service when you first download it. Create a new post; the post’s data will be sent to the S3 bucket. Then, check the bucket to verify whether it was stored successfully. Try deleting the data file in the bucket and see if the result matches the example below. When you delete the data file, it is not actually removed. Enable show version to see that the file is marked with a delete marker, but the actual data still exists.
If you attempt to delete the original file, you will get the Failed to delete objects error. This confirms that the configured Object Lock is working correctly. Wait until the Object Lock retention period expires, then try deleting the file again. After successful deletion, enable show version again; this time the file should be completely removed. When the Object Lock expired on 2025-08-06 at 22:39:15, the file became eligible to transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval according to the lifecycle rule. However, the actual transition occurred at around 21:50 on 2025-08-07 — roughly 22–23 hours later.
This happens because AWS S3 does not perform lifecycle transitions instantly; they are processed according to internal scan schedules without a fixed execution time. Therefore, in all cases, users should be aware that storage class transitions might be delayed compared to the expected time, even if the lifecycle rule is configured correctly.
Note: The data file stored in the bucket must be larger than 218KB.
If this condition is not met, the storage class transition will not occur.
You need to ensure that when creating a post, the stored data size exceeds 218KB.
Once the object has transitioned to the Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class, perform a restore to download and verify that the file’s data integrity remains intact. After a successful restore, you can either click Open to view it or Download to save it locally.
Check the expiration time of the version, and revisit later to confirm if it has expired as expected. A sign that it is working correctly is when, upon visiting the blog-micro-data-archive bucket, you see no folders or files unless show version is enabled.

title: Clean Up Resources
content:
We will follow these steps to delete the resources we created in this practice.
Delete EC2 Instance Go to the EC2 Management Console Click Instances. Click Instance state. Click Terminate instance, then click Terminate to confirm. Delete S3 Bucket Go to S3 Buckets. Select the bucket. Click Delete. Since objects still exist, you must delete all objects inside the bucket before deleting the bucket. Next: Enter permanently delete in the confirmation field. Click Empty. Continue: Enter blog-micro-data-archive in the confirmation field. Click Delete bucket.
